description: En Full Galácticos somos estudiantes de Ingeniería de Sistemas y creemos que simular la ingeniería espacial no tiene por qué ser aburrido ni ultraformal. Nos unimos para asumir el desafío de crear un juego interactivo de diseño y gestión de misiones espaciales, combinando decisiones técnicas reales con una jugabilidad atractiva y una estética visual impecable.
summary:
Space mission design is often perceived as a complex, theoretical field, making it difficult for students and the general public to understand how physical, budgetary, and environmental constraints shape real space exploration. Therefore, our objective was to create an accessible, interactive simulator that brings aerospace engineering and scientific decision-making into a hands-on experience.
GAIA is a 3D and web strategy game built in Godot Engine 4 for 1 to 4 players that addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players design a mission under strict mass and budget limits, run a role-based Go/No-Go review, and operate on Mars (Jezero Crater) and the Moon’s South Pole using official NASA 3D models and open JPL data. Finally, a post-mission report compares their results against real missions like Mars 2020 and Apollo.
Ultimately, GAIA shows that exploring other worlds requires balancing technical trade-offs, managing limited resources, and acting with scientific responsibility.
details:
GAIA is an interactive 3D and web space mission simulator built in Godot Engine 4.7.2 that challenges 1 to 4 players to design, launch, and operate robotic missions to Jezero Crater (Mars) and the Lunar South Pole. By combining real NASA 3D assets, open JPL/Artemis datasets, role-based Go/No-Go reviews, and surface survival mechanics, GAIA transforms aerospace engineering trade-offs into an accessible educational experience. Players can choose whether each sol lasts 6, 8, 10, or 12 minutes. The total session length varies with the chosen setting and how the mission unfolds.


Project Description

What Does It Do?

GAIA is an educational 3D and web simulator where 1 to 4 players design, launch, and operate robotic missions to Mars, specifically to Jezero Crater, and the Lunar South Pole. Players manage real engineering constraints—mass, power, budget, and environmental hazards—to complete scientific research and transmit data before the end of Sol 6. In multiplayer, each player drives their own rover and has their own role, all in one shared mission. Players can join a room hosted on the GAIA server or play together over the same local network.

During surface operations, players build a base with solar panels, storage, and an antenna that can be upgraded to level three. The rover drives to construction sites and welds the structures. On Mars, fictional creatures attack the base, and players defend it with turrets, walls, and a gate. Defeated creatures drop fictional bionutrients that the rover can collect and unload at the base. On the Moon, players manage energy in low sunlight and permanently shadowed areas.

How Does It Work?

  • Mission Briefing: Introduces scientific goals and destination hazards.
  • Engineering Workshop: Players configure their spacecraft within a $700M budget (plus $200M for each additional player) and launch vehicle mass limits, selecting rockets, trajectories, power sources, communications, and real NASA instruments, plus support units like Ingenuity and our companion robot, Rocky.
  • Launch, Transit & Landing: Automated flight sequence to the target surface.
  • Surface Operations (Sol 1–6): On a 1:1 scale terrain, players gather resources, build infrastructure, manage batteries through freezing nights and dust storms, and handle historical anomalies. Ethical choices—such as prioritizing resource extraction over preserving scientific sites—lead to four different endings.
  • Comparative Debrief: Compares player results across all four mission segments against real Mars 2020/Perseverance, Apollo, and Artemis data.

Innovation & Purpose

GAIA unifies hard aerospace engineering constraints with interactive storytelling inside a single adaptable engine capable of simulating two contrasting worlds: Mars’ dusty atmosphere and the Moon’s airless, extreme-shadow terrain. By letting players choose the length of each sol and introducing ethical dilemmas through Rocky, GAIA makes space mission design engaging and intuitive for non-specialists.

Benefits & Impact

A. Social, Environmental & Technological Benefits

  • Social: Gives students and educators free access to a bilingual space mission simulator they can play in a browser or download as a ready-to-run Windows game.
  • Environmental: Promotes awareness of planetary protection and responsible resource extraction via in-game ethical trade-offs.
  • Technological: Implements a clean 3-layer simulation architecture in Godot 4 validated by automated unit tests.

B. Contribution to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) & Space Missions

  • SDG 4 · Quality Education: hands-on STEM learning based on real NASA data, free and bilingual.
  • SDG 9 · Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure: promotes engineering and innovation skills and interest in space technology.
  • Space missions: brings Mars 2020/Perseverance and NASA’s lunar south pole exploration (the Artemis focus region) closer to the public.

C. Expected Community Impact

  • Inspires students, educators, and tech enthusiasts to explore STEM careers by showing that space exploration depends on teamwork, critical thinking, and ethical responsibility.

Objectives & Expected Results

General Objective: Develop an accessible and playable game that teaches space mission design using real NASA data and constraints.

Specific Objectives:

  • Model the full mission cycle: design, review, launch, cruise, landing, operations and report.
  • Use real NASA data, images and 3D models, each with its source.
  • Offer two destinations with different physics and energy conditions.
  • Support teamwork by roles, for 1 to 4 players.
  • Keep the simulation testable and data-driven, so that non-programmers can tune the balance.

Expected results: A complete, playable desktop game and a web build, an end-of-mission report comparing each mission with the real one, documentation of every NASA source, and a declaration of AI use.

Methodology & Work Plan

Project phases and main activities

Intermediate deliverables:

  • Mission design workshop with live validation of budget and mass (see Annex, Figure 3).
  • Launch platform with four real launchers at real scale (Figures 1 and 2).
  • Performance measurements before and after the art upgrade (docs/mediciones/).
  • Automated test suite (more than 670 GUT tests on the simulation and interface).

Methodology & Tools

Tools and software used

Programming language and framework

  • GDScript on Godot 4.7.2 (no .NET).
  • Data in JSON files (content/).
  • Python for asset generation scripts (textures, music, sounds, rocket models).

Hardware and sensors

GAIA is a software project that uses no sensors or special hardware. It was developed on the team’s Windows PCs. On 15 November, the desktop test on an Intel UHD integrated GPU recorded 59–60 FPS in the mission and on the launch platform. The tests ran from the Godot editor using OpenGL at 1280 × 720 on both the High and Low presets. On the same computer, Chrome took 30–50 seconds to load the game on the first visit while compiling shaders. Later visits took about 3 seconds. The full measurements are documented in docs/mediciones/ in the source repository.

Project Management

Project Location & Justification

The project was developed by team Full Galácticos at the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 local event in Cajamarca, Peru. As a digital game, it can be played anywhere: in a browser or on a Windows PC.

Team Roles

  • Kevin Jhoel Huamán Gonzales: game code and simulation, multiplayer, performance testing, server, and release.
  • Amner Jhonatan Marín Valdez: mission data, engineering workshop, rockets, and sound effects.
  • Evelin Yudith Vásquez Acosta: 3D models of rockets and buildings.
  • Jesus Arturo Valdiviezo Zavaleta: visual art, realism, and 3D models.
  • Scarlet Sahori Terrones Cerna: story development and bionutrients.
  • Dider Anthony Díaz Becerra: story, dialogue, and radio voices.

Project justification

Space mission design is usually invisible to the public and to many students, especially outside the big space centres. In regions like Cajamarca, access to hands-on STEM resources about space is limited. A free, bilingual game that runs on modest computers and uses real NASA data can bring mission design to classrooms and spark interest in science and engineering careers.

Impact & Benefits

  • Mars 2020/Perseverance: the Mars campaign uses the real launch date, 203-day cruise, rover mass, MMRTG power, instruments, signal delay and the Jezero landing site.
  • Lunar south pole: the Moon campaign reflects why NASA targets the south polar region: low Sun angles, illuminated ridges and permanently shadowed regions with water ice.
  • NASA’s four mission segments: launch, space, ground and user segments are described in the mission report using the player’s own mission.
  • STEM engagement: supports NASA’s goal of inspiring the next generation of explorers through real data.

Expected Results

  • GAIA is available as a playable web build and a downloadable desktop version for 64-bit Windows 10 and 11. To play on Windows, extract GAIA_Windows.zip and open Jugar GAIA.bat.
  • Players who understand that mass, power, communications, budget and time are linked, and can explain why their mission succeeded or failed.
  • A documented, open, data-driven codebase that other teams and students can extend.

Conclusions & Future Improvements

GAIA uses NASA mission data and engineering constraints to give players meaningful decisions. The final report compares the player’s mission with real mission data and explains which values, such as mass and cost, were adjusted for gameplay.

Lessons learned

  • A single 1:1 scale for the whole project avoided mismatches between models, terrain and buildings.
  • Keeping the data in JSON let designers and artists tune the game without touching code.
  • Separating the simulation from the visuals made it possible to test the rules automatically.
  • Integrating many branches at the end is risky; merging develop daily reduces conflicts.
  • Visual problems are not caught by tests: screenshots must be reviewed.
  • Labelling clearly what is real NASA data and what is a game value builds trust.

Possible optimisations and future work

  • Test the game with students and teachers and measure learning.
  • Test online multiplayer across different computers and networks.
  • Decide and build the telescope (instrument or space telescope mission).
  • More realistic trajectories (for example with NASA’s GMAT) and Concept Maturity Levels.
  • Measure performance on more GPUs.
  • Reduce the initial loading time of the browser version on computers with integrated graphics.

Use of AI

Team Full Galácticos declares the use of AI in this project. The idea, game design, rules, decisions and supervision are the team’s. The team created the architecture and base classes first, following a Godot book; AI then wrote a large part of the code under the team’s direction.

  • Claude (Anthropic): Claude contributed much of the game code and documentation under the team’s direction. It wrote Blender scripts to generate procedural textures, repair crystal and mineral meshes, and build the mountain range on the horizon. It also wrote a Python script that generated the Delta II, Titan IIIE-Centaur, and Atlas V 541 models, and another that synthesized the orchestral layer mixed with the team’s own GAIA theme. Claude also helped edit the trailer and prepare the presentation slides.
  • Codex: Implementation and tests of the fictional bionutrient deposits; bilingual writing and integration of story scripts; mixing of the radio voices; integration of the Fault expedition and optional station.
  • Canva AI image generator: Used through the Claude desktop app to create the GAIA logo, the main menu background, the loading screen, the launch platform background, and the story illustrations. Each AI-generated image carries the visible label “Imagen generada con IA · AI-generated”.
  • Radio voice synthesis The English dialogue uses Piper’s John and Joe voices. The Spanish story dialogue uses Microsoft Raúl and Microsoft Pablo from Windows speech synthesis. Some additional Houston lines use the Mexican Spanish Piper voice “ald”. The clips were processed with a walkie-talkie effect.
